CHAPTER 1
INTRODUCTION

In the modern business environment, the efficient management of store operations plays a vital role in ensuring the smooth functioning of manufacturing and trading organizations. Handling procurement, inventory, material movement, and billing through manual or paper-based methods is time-consuming, error-prone, and lacks transparency. There is an urgent need for a reliable, digital solution that brings all these operations under one unified platform.

The Store Management System is a comprehensive, full-stack web application designed to digitize and automate the complete lifecycle of store operations from raising purchase orders to issuing materials to departments. The system was developed to meet the real-world operational requirements of KR Exports, a trading and export organization, and is deployed in a live production environment.

The application is organized into three major functional domains: Master Data Management, which covers all foundational records such as items, suppliers, departments, and stores; Transaction Management, which handles day-to-day operations including purchase orders, gate inwards, receipts, bill entries, item issues, and gate passes; and Reports & Analytics, which provides management with real-time visibility into all store activities through dynamic, exportable reports.

The system is hosted at https://krexports.org and is supported by a Jenkins-based CI/CD pipeline for automated builds and deployments, making it production-ready and maintainable. This report documents the design, development, and implementation of the Store Management System, providing a complete technical overview of its architecture, features, and functionality.
CHAPTER 2
OBJECTIVES
To Digitize Store Operations: Replace manual record-keeping with a digital system to improve accuracy, efficiency, and data accessibility.
To Centralize Master Data: Maintain consistent and accurate master data for items, departments, suppliers, stores, and other entities.
To Automate the Procurement Lifecycle: Streamline procurement from purchase orders to bill verification with complete traceability.
To Track Material Movement: Monitor and record all inward and outward movement of goods for effective inventory control.
To Manage Item Issuance to Departments: Record item issuance to departments to ensure accountability and proper stock management.
To Enforce User Authentication and Role-Based Access: Secure the application using JWT authentication and protected routes to prevent unauthorized access.
To Provide Dynamic Reporting and Analytics: Generate detailed reports and export them to Excel for effective analysis and decision-making.
To Ensure System Security and Reliability: Implement security measures such as Helmet, CORS, rate limiting, and payload restrictions to protect the system.
To Deploy a Scalable, Maintainable Architecture: Use a modular REST API architecture with separate frontend, backend, and database layers for easier maintenance and scalability.
To Enable Continuous Deployment via CI/CD: Automate application builds and deployments using Jenkins for consistent and efficient production updates at KR Exports.
CHAPTER 3
DESCRIPTION
The Store Management System is a full-stack web application developed to manage and automate store and inventory operations at KR Exports. The system consists of five major functional areas:
1. Master Data Management

This module maintains centralized master records, including departments, suppliers, stores, items, product heads and sub-heads, units of measure (UOM), parties, purchase types, and states. These records ensure consistency and accuracy across all store transactions.
2. Transaction Management

This module manages day-to-day store activities, including Purchase Orders, Gate Inward, Material Receipts, Bill Entry, Bill Verification, Item Issue, Gate Pass In, Gate Pass Out, and Purchase Order Cancellation. Each transaction is linked to relevant master data, ensuring traceability, accountability, and effective inventory control.
3. Reports and Dashboard

The Reports module generates dynamic reports for purchase orders, receipts, item issues, bills, and gate pass activities using filters such as date, department, supplier, and item. Reports can be exported to Excel for further analysis. The Dashboard provides an overview of pending orders and recent store activities.
4. Security and Access Control

The system uses bcrypt for password hashing and JSON Web Token (JWT) authentication to secure user access. Protected API routes, Axios response interceptors, and request rate limiting help prevent unauthorized access and manage invalid or expired sessions.
5. Technology and Deployment

The application uses React for the frontend, Node.js for the backend, and MySQL with Sequelize for database management. It is deployed at https://krexports.orgsvg, with a Jenkins CI/CD pipeline automating application builds and deployments. The modular architecture supports maintainability, scalability, and future enhancements.

MODULES
8.0 Design Approach

Each module of the Store Management System is described here the way a system design problem is solved: by walking through the same seven steps in the same order, every time. This keeps the explanation of every module complete and comparable, and shows why each design decision was taken rather than only what the screen looks like.
Shared baseline for all modules

Non-functional baseline. Every request travels through Helmet (HTTP hardening), CORS, a payload size limit, a rate limiter and the JWT authentication middleware before it reaches a controller. All data lives in a single MySQL database, so the system chooses consistency over availability in CAP terms (CP): a user may briefly be unable to save if the database is unreachable, but two users can never see conflicting versions of a purchase order or a stock balance. Money columns use DECIMAL, never floating point, so totals reconcile exactly.
Sizing baseline (assumptions).

A single Node.js process and one MySQL instance handle this load comfortably. The design keeps the application stateless (JWT instead of server sessions), so extra Node.js instances can be added behind a load balancer if usage grows.

8.2 USER AUTHENTICATION & ACCESS CONTROL
8.2.0 Purpose & Scope
Provides tokenized authentication, secure credential management, and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) across the enterprise, preventing unauthorized data modifications.
8.2.1 Functional Requirements
What the module must do:
A user signs in with a username and password and receives a signed JWT plus a profile (id, full_name, role).
A signed-in user can change their own password; administrators can register new users.
Four roles – admin, manager, operator, viewer – decide which endpoints a user may call.
Each account has an active / inactive status so access can be withdrawn without deleting the record, and the last login time is stored.
The browser redirects unauthenticated users to the login screen (protected routes) and handles an expired or invalid token centrally.
Out of scope: self-service sign-up, social login / SSO and multi-factor authentication.
8.2.2 Non-Functional Requirements
How well the module must do it (the system-wide baseline in the chapter introduction also applies):
Security: passwords are stored only as bcryptjs hashes with auto-generated salts; the hash is never returned by the API.
Brute-force defence: at most 15 login attempts per 15 minutes per IP address on /api/auth/login.
Session length: tokens expire after 12 hours, which limits the damage of a stolen token while avoiding repeated logins in one shift.
Scalability: because tokens are stateless, any server instance can validate a request without a shared session store.
Latency target: login under 500 ms (dominated by the deliberate cost of bcrypt); token verification adds only microseconds per request.
CAP: the user table is a single MySQL source of truth – consistency is preferred, so a disabled account is refused immediately on the next login.

8.2.5 Low-Level Architecture
Fig 8.2.A Low-level architecture – USER AUTHENTICATION & ACCESS CONTROL
Request flow:
Login.jsx posts the credentials; rateLimiter.js counts the attempt for the caller’s IP.
authController looks the user up by username (unique index), checks that the status is active, and compares the password with the stored bcrypt hash.
On success it updates last_login, signs a JWT (12 h) and returns the token with the profile.
The client stores the token; api.js adds it as a Bearer header on every later request.
auth.js verifies the signature and expiry and checks the role before the route handler runs.
A 401 response triggers the Axios interceptor, which clears the session and sends the user back to the login screen.
8.2.6 API Design
Only /api/auth/login is public. The remaining paths are representative routes derived from the authController methods.
8.2.7 DB Design
The unique index on username makes the login look-up a single index read and prevents duplicate accounts.
No other table has a foreign key to Users, so authentication can be changed independently of the store data.

8.3 MASTER DATA MANAGEMENT
8.3.0 Purpose & Scope
Unifies foundational reference datasets and enterprise catalogs that establish the baseline for all store operations, inventory classification, and vendor management.
8.3.1 Functional Requirements
What the module must do:
Create, view, edit and delete records for: Item, Supplier, Department, Store Master, Product Head, Sub Head, UOM, State, Purchase Type, Party Master and Item Master (gate-pass items).
Central item catalog: item code, name, department, sub head, UOM, unit rate, opening stock, min / max stock level (reorder level), HSN code, location.
Supplier registry: account name, place, address, delivery address, GSTIN, PAN, contact details and opening credit / debit.
Search and filter large lists: suppliers by department, place and GST status; items by department, sub head and UOM; sorting and page size.
Bulk upload of items from a CSV file.
Purchase Type records carry accounting formulas (assessable value, round off, lorry freight) and SGST / CGST / IGST / TCS ledger mappings.
Provide searchable reference dropdowns to every transaction screen so users pick, rather than type, master values.
8.3.2 Non-Functional Requirements
How well the module must do it (the system-wide baseline in the chapter introduction also applies):
Read-heavy: masters are read many times more often than they are changed (roughly 100 reads per write), so look-ups must be fast.
Scale of lists: with 5,490 suppliers and 11,011 items, lists are paginated on the server (10 per page by default) and never loaded whole.
Data quality: unique keys on department name, state name, store name and purchase type prevent duplicates; item and sub head records link to their parent through department_id / SubHeadCode.
Access control: write endpoints are restricted by role (for example, the viewer role is read-only).
CAP: consistency first – a new supplier or item must be visible to every user as soon as it is saved, because transactions depend on it immediately.

8.4 PURCHASE ORDER (PO) MANAGEMENT
8.4.0 Purpose & Scope
Orchestrates the procurement lifecycle, from raising purchase orders with approved vendors to multi-item price calculations, status tracking, and authorized order cancellations.
8.4.1 Functional Requirements
What the module must do:
Raise a PO for a supplier: order date, party, address / place, reference number and remarks; the PO number (for example PO-772) is generated automatically in sequence.
Multi-item line engine: each line takes item, quantity, unit rate, discount %, GST type (SGST + CGST or IGST), packing & forwarding, lorry freight and MRS number, and shows the line total instantly.
Order summary: items subtotal, total discount, total tax, P&F, lorry freight, round off and grand total.
Lifecycle tracking: Draft → Pending / Approval → Approved → Inward Created → Completed / Cancelled.
Register: search by order number, party or reference; filter by party and status; sort; expand a row to see its lines; copy, edit or delete a PO.
Controlled cancellation: a PO is cancelled only with a mandatory reason, and not once its items have arrived at the gate.
8.4.2 Non-Functional Requirements
How well the module must do it (the system-wide baseline in the chapter introduction also applies):

Accuracy: amounts are DECIMAL(15,2) and unit rates DECIMAL(15,6), so a PO total always matches the sum of its lines. Example (Fig 8.4.3–8.4.4): ₹20,000 − ₹1,800 discount = ₹18,200; GST is 18 % of (₹18,200 + ₹5,000 P&F + ₹5,000 freight) = ₹5,076; grand total = ₹18,200 + ₹5,000 + ₹5,000 + ₹5,076 = ₹33,276.
Atomicity: the header and all its lines are saved together in one transaction; a PO never exists half-saved.
Unique numbering: the PO number is allocated on the server and the primary key is the final guard against duplicates when two clerks save at the same time.
Server-side validation: totals sent by the browser are recomputed on the server before saving.
Auditability: every cancellation stores a reason and date; all tables carry createdAt / updatedAt.
Responsiveness: the register opens in under 1 second; line details load only when a row is expanded.
CAP: consistency first – the status of a PO must be identical for the store, accounts and management at all times.

8.5 GOODS INWARD & INVENTORY RECEIPT (GRN)
8.5.0 Purpose & Scope
Manages the physical arrival of materials. Combines gate consignment logging with formal Goods Receipt Note (GRN) stock induction.
8.5.1 Functional Requirements
What the module must do:
Gate Inward: log an arrival with an automatic inward number (for example GI-771), inward date, party, the purchase order being delivered, and the supplier’s invoice number and date.
Record received quantity against pending quantity for each PO line; one PO can have several inward batches (partial deliveries).
Duplicate invoice check: warn when the same supplier invoice is entered twice.

Receipt (GRN): select party and PO, pick the gate-inward batches covered, add invoice, DC number and dates, confirm received items with rate, and enter discount, GST, P&F, lorry freight and round off to get the grand total.
Receiving goods updates the stock balance of the received items and advances the PO status to Inward Created / Completed.
Registers with search, party filter and sort; expand a GRN to trace it back to its gate inward and PO; edit and delete (the delete removes the linked chain consistently).
8.5.2 Non-Functional Requirements
How well the module must do it (the system-wide baseline in the chapter introduction also applies):
Traceability: PO → Gate Inward → GRN is linked by OrderNo and GateInwardNo, so any stock line can be traced to the order that created it.
Integrity: received quantity cannot exceed what is still pending on the PO line; the same invoice cannot be booked twice.
Atomic chain operations: creating a GRN (header, lines, stock update, status change) and deleting a chain run in one transaction.
Responsiveness: the dependent dropdowns (party → open POs → PO items) answer in under 500 ms.
Auditability: createdAt / updatedAt on every row; status values (Draft, InwardCreated) show progress.
CAP: consistency first – stock must never be counted twice or lost if two users receive against the same PO.

8.6 BILL ENTRY
8.6.0 Purpose & Scope
Handles financial booking of supplier invoices against physically received goods, and records the verification of each booked bill before payment.
8.6.1 Functional Requirements
What the module must do:
Book a supplier invoice against a received GRN: pick the party, then the linked gate inward / GRN; the voucher number (for example VCH-769) is generated automatically.
Capture party bill number, bill date, accounting date and purchase type; the narration is pre-filled (“Being Supply of … as per Bill no …”).

Show billed items (item, PO, quantity, rate, amount) taken from the GRN, with a financial breakdown: subtotal, discount, GST, IGST, VAT / CST, P&F, lorry freight, round off, TDS / TCS and grand total (bill amount).
Support both intra-state (CGST + SGST) and inter-state (IGST) tax amounts.
Three-way traceability: PO, GRN and bill are linked, so the ordered rate, the received quantity and the billed amount can be compared.
Duplicate bill check, edit, delete (with the linked chain) and print of the voucher.
Bill Verify: record the verification date, payment status and remarks for each booked bill.
8.6.2 Non-Functional Requirements
How well the module must do it (the system-wide baseline in the chapter introduction also applies):
No double billing: the schema enforces one bill per GRN and per gate inward through unique keys.
Financial accuracy: all amounts are DECIMAL(15,2); the grand total is recomputed on the server.
Atomicity: bill header, billed lines and the chain delete run in one transaction.
Auditability: accounting date, voucher number, verification date and remarks are stored for each bill.
Print performance: a voucher renders in under 1 second.
CAP: consistency first – the accounts team must always see the same bill amount as the store.

8.7 MATERIAL REQUISITION & GATE PASS MOVEMENT
8.7.0 Purpose & Scope
Controls internal inventory consumption by departments and regulates the physical outbound / inbound movement of tools, machinery, and non-inventory goods through the gate.
8.7.1 Functional Requirements
What the module must do:
Item Issue: create an issue voucher (for example ISS-0004) with date, department, indent number, approver / issued-by and remarks.
Show the department’s items with available stock and a status badge (In stock, Low stock, Out of stock); the user enters an issue quantity that must not exceed the stock.
Filter the item list, see the count of selected items and total units, then confirm & save; the stock balance is reduced by the issued quantity.
Edit or delete an existing issue; list issues by department.
Gate Pass Out / In: record tools, machinery and non-inventory goods leaving or re-entering the premises with party, items and quantities.
Returnable (RGP) and non-returnable (NRGP) passes, and return reconciliation of items coming back against open passes.
8.7.2 Non-Functional Requirements
How well the module must do it (the system-wide baseline in the chapter introduction also applies):
Stock integrity: stock must never go negative – the quantity is validated on the server inside a transaction that locks the item rows being issued.
Concurrency: two storekeepers issuing the same item at the same moment are serialized by the row lock, so the second sees the reduced balance.
Usability: a department can have hundreds of items; the list is filterable and shows the remaining stock as the user types.
Accountability: each issue stores the department, indent number, approver and employee name for every line.
CAP: consistency first – an out-of-date stock figure would allow over-issue, so correctness outranks availability.

8.8 EXECUTIVE DASHBOARD & BUSINESS ANALYTICS
8.8.0 Purpose & Scope
Provides operational transparency and business intelligence through live KPI monitoring and multi-criteria transactional report generation with spreadsheet and document exports.
8.8.1 Functional Requirements
What the module must do:
Dashboard KPI cards: active purchase orders, items in stock, gate passes outward and pending verifications, with a manual refresh.
Monthly transactions chart (POs, gate-in, gate-out), a status overview and the recent gate inward log.
Low-stock alerts: flag items whose stock has fallen to or below the configured minimum (OpeningQty ≤ MinStockLevel).
Reports & Registers in six categories – Purchase, Billing, Receipt, Stock, Issue and Others – each with a named report (for example Department Wise Order Details, Date wise receipt register).
Filters: from / to date, report name, department (multi-select), party and item; preview on screen, then save.
Export: formatted Excel (.xlsx) workbooks built with ExcelJS, and printable PDF documents.
8.8.2 Non-Functional Requirements
How well the module must do it (the system-wide baseline in the chapter introduction also applies):
Read-only: the module never modifies transactional data, so it cannot corrupt stock or bills.
Performance: a one-year report completes in under 3 seconds and the dashboard in under 2 seconds.
Memory safety: large exports are streamed to the browser instead of being assembled fully in memory.
Freshness: figures reflect committed data; the Refresh button re-queries on demand rather than polling.
Scalability path: heavy reports can move to a MySQL read replica later without changing the API.
CAP: consistency preferred – a report must match what the transaction screens show.

CHAPTER 9
CONCLUSION

The Store Management System provides a complete digital solution for managing the major activities involved in store and inventory operations. The system integrates master data management, purchase orders, gate inward entries, goods receipts, bill processing, item issues, gate passes, dashboards, and reports within a single application. By replacing manual records and disconnected processes, it improves the accuracy, consistency, and accessibility of operational information. The application was developed using React for the frontend, Node.js and Express for the backend, and MySQL with Sequelize for database management. Its client-server architecture supports structured communication between the user interface, application server, and database. JWT authentication, password hashing, role-based access control, request rate limiting, and protected routes help secure the system and prevent unauthorized access. The completed project demonstrates how a web-based information system can simplify store operations, reduce repetitive work, minimize recording errors, and improve decision-making. Its modular structure makes the application easier to maintain and allows additional features to be introduced in the future. Overall, the Store Management System successfully meets its objective of providing a secure, organized, and efficient platform for managing store activities at KR Exports.
